versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 34 Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me. 35 For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.

36 What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul? 37 Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul? 38 If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.”

context_lines: Jesus calls the crowd alongside His disciples, so this teaching reaches beyond Peter or the Twelve. It follows His announcement of suffering, death, and resurrection. He now describes what it means for someone to come after Him: deny oneself, take up a cross, and follow.

The cross is a severe image. [Mark 15:21–24](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/15.htm) later narrates a cross being carried on the way to Jesus' crucifixion. In this call, loyalty to Jesus and the gospel can cost security, standing, and even life. The issue is how a person responds when following Him carries a price.

Jesus then turns ordinary ideas of gain and loss upside down. A person can preserve what seems most valuable now and lose what matters most, or lose life for His sake and the gospel and save it. Possessing the whole world cannot pay for the life forfeited in the exchange.

The same Greek noun, [ψυχή (psyche, psoo-KHAY)](https://biblehub.com/greek/5590.htm), appears where the BSB uses life in verse 35 and soul in verses 36–37. Its range includes life and the person or soul; the connection makes Jesus' questions one joined warning. The word alone does not settle every dispute about salvation and rewards.

The final warning looks toward the Son of Man's coming in His Father's glory with the angels. Shame about Jesus and His words is set against His response then. The teaching asks hearers to weigh present acceptance against their relationship to Him and the future He announces.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians agree that this is a serious call to costly loyalty. They differ over how the warning about saving or losing life relates to salvation and rewards.

In Reformed teaching, the [Westminster Confession, 11.2](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html), and the [1689 Baptist Confession, 11.2](https://www.the1689confession.com/1689/chapter-11), teach that a person is put right with God through faith alone, and that this is a living faith that works through love. [Calvin's reading of this passage](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/8.htm) connects losing earthly life for Christ with eternal life. Those confessions do not present obedience as the price paid to earn acceptance by God.

The Catholic [Catechism, 1816](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_one/chapter_one/article_7/ii_the_theological_virtues.html), says disciples must live their faith, confess Christ, and follow the way of the cross. It describes service and witness to faith as necessary for salvation. The Catholic [USCCB note on Mark 8:34–35](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/mark/8) reads loyalty to Christ, even through death, in relation to fullness of life, and life spent denying Him in relation to destruction.

[Wesley on Mark 8:34](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-mark/) describes self-denial as continually yielding to God's will, including when it is painful. The Methodist [Articles of Religion, XII](https://www.umc.org/en/content/articles-of-religion), teach that believers can depart from grace and, through God's grace, return. This framework differs from readings that hold salvation secure while addressing a believer's future rewards.

Some Free Grace teachers make a different distinction. In the [Grace Evangelical Society's discussion of Mark 8:34–38](https://faithalone.org/radio/save-your-life-by-losing-it-mark-834-38/), the warning concerns believers' discipleship, future reward, and honor rather than obtaining or losing eternal salvation. This is an identifiable reading within that movement, not a position shared by every evangelical or Baptist.
god_plan_lines: Jesus' call follows the pattern of His own self-giving. [Philippians 2:5–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/philippians/2.htm) calls believers to His way of thinking, then describes His humility, obedience to death on a cross, and exaltation by God. The connection between suffering and glory gives a larger setting for the cost and future Jesus places before His hearers.

[2 Timothy 1:8–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_timothy/1.htm) joins the same themes: do not be ashamed, share in suffering for the gospel, and trust the Savior who has defeated death. It also describes salvation as God's purpose and grace rather than the result of our works. Paul's willingness to count loss for the sake of knowing Christ in [Philippians 3:7–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/philippians/3.htm) shows that this call became part of the lived witness of the early church.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
